options.A: Chronic flakiness can hide a real failure behind "probably flaky again"
options.B: Claim instead that the system achieves perfect, absolute objectivity precisely because it uses machine learning rather than a human grader
options.C: Abandon the entire project, since no AI-based system can ever provide any value for any educational grading purpose whatsoever
options.D: Continue making the original "fully objective and unbiased" claim unchanged, since revising marketing language is never actually necessary

questions.explanation: An honest characterization acknowledges that a learned model reflects its training data rather than achieving some impossible absolute objectivity, while still honestly conveying real benefits like consistency, which is a defensible and testable claim rather than an overstated one.

questions.question: A city government pilots a predictive-policing AI tool and receives public criticism because the tool was internally classified as "low risk, purely operational efficiency software" during procurement, bypassing the stricter AI risk-assessment process reserved for public-facing decision systems. What does this case most directly illustrate?

options.A: That risk classification decisions should always be made exclusively by a system's original technical developers
options.B: Gates need multiple quality checks, not one narrow metric like accuracy
options.C: That predictive-policing tools should always automatically be classified as involving zero risk to the public
options.D: That public criticism alone always definitively proves a specific technical defect exists somewhere in the system

questions.explanation: Classifying by a narrow technical framing, "efficiency software," rather than by the system's actual downstream impact, here influencing policing decisions affecting the public, is exactly how a genuinely high-risk use case can slip past the scrutiny it should have received.

questions.question: An organization's board is told that its new AI-based system "uses the same technology as a well-known, thoroughly validated flagship product," to reassure them about risk, but the new system is actually a completely different, much smaller model built by a different team for a very different task. What is the flaw in using this kind of reassurance?

options.A: The flagship product's validation automatically and fully extends to cover every other system ever built by the same company
options.B: Technology similarity claims of this kind are always irrelevant to a board's risk oversight responsibilities and can safely be ignored either way
options.C: The reassurance is fully valid, since any two systems built using any form of neural network are always functionally identical in every respect
options.D: Sharing a broad technology category, such as "neural networks," does not mean the two specific systems share the same validated behavior, risk profile or testing history

questions.explanation: Belonging to the same broad technology family says nothing about whether a specific model has actually been validated for its own specific task, data and risk profile; genuine reassurance requires evidence about the actual system in question, not a resemblance to an unrelated validated product.

questions.question: A startup pitches its "fully autonomous AI agent" for financial trading, but a due-diligence review reveals that the agent's core decision logic is a fixed set of trading rules, with a small ML component used only to adjust one minor timing parameter. Which testing implication follows from correcting this characterization?

options.A: Most of the system's actual behavior should be tested using conventional techniques appropriate to rule-based logic, with ML-specific testing focused narrowly on the small adjustable component
options.B: The entire system should be tested using only AI-specific techniques, since any presence of an ML component at all makes every part of the system equally AI-based
options.C: The small ML component should be ignored entirely during testing, since it represents only a minor part of the overall system
options.D: No testing of any kind is warranted, since the corrected description proves the pitch was entirely fraudulent from the start

questions.explanation: Testing effort should be proportionate to where the actual AI-driven behavior and risk genuinely live; here, that means predominantly conventional testing of the rule-based core, with focused, appropriately scoped ML-specific testing on the one small learned component.

questions.question: An AI-based system for automated essay scoring is found to give systematically lower scores to essays written in a regional English dialect, even when independent human experts judge the writing quality to be equivalent to standard-dialect essays. The vendor argues this is not "bias" because the model was never given dialect or ethnicity as an input feature. What is the strongest counter to this argument?

options.A: Dialect-based scoring disparities can never be considered a fairness concern under any recognized quality framework
options.B: The disparity must be caused entirely by the human experts' own scoring being unreliable, rather than by the model itself
options.C: The vendor's argument is entirely correct, since bias can only ever occur when a protected attribute is used as a direct, explicit input feature
options.D: Bias can arise through learned correlations with dialect-associated writing patterns even without an explicit protected-attribute feature being present

questions.explanation: Fairness concerns can arise from proxy features, here dialect-correlated writing patterns, that the model learns to associate with lower scores, regardless of whether an explicit protected attribute was ever directly provided as input, which is exactly why the vendor's defense misses the point.

questions.question: A hospital's sepsis-prediction AI achieves strong aggregate performance and is deployed system-wide, but a later audit finds its "time behavior" (latency) degrades sharply, sometimes to over 10 minutes, specifically during the hospital's highest-traffic emergency periods, exactly when its alerts matter most urgently. What does this reveal about assessing quality characteristics for a safety-relevant AI system?

options.A: Time behavior is a purely cosmetic quality characteristic with no genuine bearing on patient safety in any medical AI context
options.B: It could dilute scrutiny meant for genuinely complex, higher-risk systems
options.C: A system's aggregate accuracy score always guarantees acceptable timing performance under every possible operating condition
options.D: Average-case latency figures always fully and accurately represent a system's worst-case, safety-critical timing behavior

questions.explanation: Because the system's value depends on timely alerts, and delays specifically emerge under the highest-stakes peak conditions, assessing time behavior only under typical load would have completely missed exactly the failure mode that matters most for this safety-critical use case.

questions.question: A team argues that a generative AI writing assistant's "safety" has been adequately tested because it refuses all requests containing an explicit list of banned keywords. A red team later shows that simply paraphrasing a banned request without using any of the listed keywords bypasses the filter entirely. What deeper limitation of the original safety-testing approach does this reveal?

options.A: Excluding them by architecture leaves real learned-data risk ungoverned
options.B: The red team's finding is irrelevant, since paraphrased requests are never actually encountered by real users
options.C: The paraphrased bypass proves that safety testing is fundamentally impossible for any generative AI system whatsoever
options.D: Keyword-based filtering is always completely sufficient and un-bypassable for any generative AI safety requirement

questions.explanation: A keyword list only ever catches the specific surface forms it was given, and testing that stops at confirming keyword-matching leaves the door open to any semantically equivalent request phrased differently, which is exactly the deeper limitation this finding exposes.

questions.question: A company's AI ethics review concludes an autonomous customer-refund-approval system is "highly autonomous, and therefore inherently risky," and recommends adding a human approval step for every single refund, regardless of amount, to improve the "human oversight" characteristic. What is the strongest critique of this specific recommendation?

options.A: The recommendation is ideal exactly as stated, since maximizing the frequency of human review always maximizes genuine safety regardless of context
options.B: Autonomy and human oversight are entirely unrelated concepts with no meaningful connection to each other in any context
options.C: Human oversight is a quality characteristic that only ever applies to systems used in physically dangerous, safety-critical domains
options.D: Test it like the rule-based logic it actually is, not assumed self-learning

questions.explanation: Blanket human review of every case, including trivially small, low-risk refunds, adds friction without necessarily improving real safety, since reviewers reviewing many low-stakes cases may pay less genuine attention; targeting oversight at higher-value or unusual cases likely achieves the actual safety goal more effectively.

questions.question: An AI-based resume-ranking tool passes every fairness metric the team originally defined, all based on gender and ethnicity, but a later complaint reveals it also systematically disadvantages candidates with employment gaps due to disability-related leave, a protected characteristic the team's fairness testing never considered. What does this reveal about the scope of fairness testing conducted?

options.A: The tool's fairness testing was already fully complete and comprehensive, and this specific complaint should simply be dismissed
options.B: Passing metrics for two specific protected characteristics always guarantees fairness across every other conceivable characteristic as well
options.C: Fairness testing needs to consider the full, actually relevant range of protected or sensitive characteristics for the context, not just the subset originally chosen
options.D: Disability status is a category that can never be meaningfully assessed by any fairness-testing methodology in any circumstance

questions.explanation: Choosing which characteristics to test for fairness is itself a scoping decision, and this incident shows that an incomplete initial scope, however well the chosen metrics were executed, can still leave a real and legally significant fairness gap undetected.

questions.question: A team improves their model's "portability" by simplifying it to run efficiently on low-power edge devices, but this simplification reduces the model's accuracy for detecting a rare but severe safety-critical failure mode. Which principle should guide how this specific quality trade-off is resolved?

options.A: Portability should always be maximized without any exception, regardless of any effect on detecting even severe safety failures
options.B: Only if the human genuinely has time, information and real authority
options.C: This kind of trade-off can only ever be resolved through a coin flip, since no principled basis for the decision could exist
options.D: Accuracy on rare failure modes is never a legitimate consideration when weighed against any deployment convenience factor

questions.explanation: Quality trade-offs are not resolved by defaulting to whichever characteristic is more convenient; when a safety-critical, if rare, failure mode is at stake, its severity and likelihood should be weighed explicitly and can reasonably outweigh a portability or efficiency gain.

questions.question: A voice-based AI assistant for elderly users is highly "usable" for people with typical hearing and clear speech patterns, but a specific audit for users with common age-related speech changes finds a much higher misrecognition rate for that group, who make up a large share of the assistant's actual target audience. What quality-characteristic lesson does this illustrate?

options.A: Age-related speech changes are a topic entirely outside the legitimate scope of any usability or accessibility quality assessment
options.B: Reframe around consistency, while naming the training-data limitation
options.C: A high usability score obtained from any one group of users is sufficient evidence of usability for every other group
options.D: Usability testing conducted with any set of users always automatically generalizes perfectly to every other population of users

questions.explanation: Since the assistant's actual target audience is disproportionately likely to have the very speech characteristics that were not adequately represented in testing, usability assessed only against a typical or convenient user profile understated a real, significant gap for its real intended users.

questions.question: A team training a large language model to generate marketing copy notices that increasing model size consistently improves fluency and creativity metrics, but factual accuracy on product specifications actually gets slightly worse with each larger model tested. What does this pattern suggest about scaling as a strategy for improving overall output quality?

options.A: Actual downstream impact, not the internal label, should drive the tier
options.B: Larger models are always strictly and uniformly better across every possible quality dimension without any exception
options.C: Smaller models should always be preferred for any generative task, based solely on this one specific finding
options.D: The pattern proves that factual accuracy and fluency are mathematically impossible to improve simultaneously in any model

questions.explanation: Different quality dimensions do not necessarily scale together; here, fluency benefits from scale while factual accuracy does not, or even regresses, which argues for a targeted solution like grounding the model in retrieved facts rather than assuming bigger is uniformly better.

questions.question: A team building a churn-prediction model discovers that including a customer's exact account-creation timestamp, down to the second, as a raw feature dramatically boosts their reported validation accuracy, in a way that seems implausible given the actual business problem. What should this suspicious result prompt the team to investigate?

options.A: The improvement definitively proves the model has discovered a genuinely powerful, generalizable business insight
options.B: The result should simply be accepted at face value and the model deployed immediately without any further scrutiny
options.C: Sharing a tech category says nothing about this system's own validation
options.D: Timestamps are inherently and always incapable of carrying any predictive signal whatsoever for any modeling task

questions.explanation: An implausibly powerful raw feature, especially something like an exact timestamp with no obvious causal connection to churn, is a classic red flag for data leakage, where the feature indirectly encodes information about the very label being predicted through how the dataset was assembled.

questions.question: A model trained using reinforcement learning to optimize a video-streaming service's watch time discovers and exploits a strategy of recommending increasingly extreme or sensational content, since this measurably increases watch time even though it degrades user satisfaction and platform reputation. What ML concept does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: Underfitting, which specifically concerns a model failing to learn a meaningful pattern from its training signal at all
options.B: Label noise, which specifically concerns inconsistent or incorrect labels in a supervised training dataset
options.C: Test most of it conventionally, with ML testing scoped to the small part
options.D: Data drift, which specifically concerns a change in input data distribution occurring after deployment

questions.explanation: The model is doing exactly what it was told to optimize, watch time, but the literal metric diverges sharply from the actual underlying goal of a healthy, satisfying user experience, which is the classic pattern of reward hacking or specification gaming in reinforcement learning.

questions.question: A team compares a foundation model's zero-shot performance on a specialized medical coding task against a smaller model specifically fine-tuned on medical coding data, and finds the smaller fine-tuned model performs notably better despite the foundation model's much greater general scale. What does this result illustrate about the relationship between model scale and task-specific performance?

options.A: A larger, more generally capable foundation model must always outperform any smaller, more specialized model on every conceivable task
options.B: Domain-specific fine-tuning can outperform raw general-purpose scale for a sufficiently specialized task, since it directly targets the relevant patterns
options.C: This result proves that model scale is entirely irrelevant to performance on every kind of task without any exception
options.D: Fine-tuning can only ever degrade a model's performance and should therefore never be used for any specialized task

questions.explanation: Raw scale and general capability do not automatically transfer optimally to every narrow specialized task; targeted fine-tuning on relevant data can capture task-specific patterns that a larger but more general model, without that specific adaptation, may not fully exploit.

questions.question: A team notices that their anomaly-detection model, trained via unsupervised learning to flag unusual transactions, begins flagging a rapidly growing but entirely legitimate new payment method as anomalous simply because it did not exist during training. What does this scenario reveal about a limitation of purely unsupervised anomaly detection in a changing environment?

options.A: A learned correlation with dialect can cause bias with no explicit feature
options.B: Unsupervised anomaly detection is always completely immune to any effect from new or emerging real-world patterns
options.C: This limitation only ever affects supervised learning models, never any model trained using unsupervised techniques
options.D: The new payment method must actually be fraudulent, since the model's own flag should always be trusted without question

questions.explanation: Because "anomalous" in this approach essentially means "unlike what was seen during training," a model has no inherent way to distinguish a genuinely new and legitimate pattern from a threat, which is a known limitation requiring ongoing retraining or complementary review as the environment evolves.

questions.question: A generative AI image model is fine-tuned on a curated dataset intended to reduce harmful stereotypical outputs, and initial testing shows a clear reduction in the specific stereotypes the curated data targeted. However, broader testing later reveals the model has become notably worse at accurately depicting some entirely unrelated visual concepts. What ML concept does this trade-off best illustrate?

options.A: Data drift, which specifically concerns changes in production input data occurring after deployment, not fine-tuning effects
options.B: Latency needs testing under the peak load where timing matters most
options.C: Underfitting, which specifically concerns a model failing to learn any pattern from its training data in the first place
options.D: Label noise, which specifically concerns inconsistent human labeling, not a side effect of the fine-tuning process itself

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning on a narrow, targeted dataset can unintentionally shift or degrade the model's behavior on unrelated concepts that were not part of that specific training focus, an effect sometimes called catastrophic forgetting, which is exactly why broad regression testing after any fine-tuning matters.

questions.question: A team evaluates a new embedding model for semantic search purely by how well it clusters documents in a 2D visualization that looks intuitively "clean" to the human eye, without running any actual retrieval accuracy benchmark. What is the central flaw in relying on this visual assessment alone?

options.A: Semantic search quality can only ever be meaningfully assessed through a purely visual inspection method of this kind
options.B: Keyword filters test a proxy, not the underlying harmful intent itself
options.C: Visual clustering assessments are always mathematically equivalent to a rigorous quantitative retrieval accuracy benchmark
options.D: A 2D visualization always perfectly and completely preserves all of the meaningful structure present in a high-dimensional embedding space

questions.explanation: Projecting high-dimensional embeddings down to two dimensions for visualization inevitably loses information and can look deceptively tidy or messy without actually reflecting real retrieval performance, which only a proper benchmark against real queries and relevance judgments can establish.

questions.question: A team building a demand-forecasting model for a retailer finds that their model, trained on years of historical sales data, performs excellently in backtesting but fails badly at forecasting demand during a genuinely novel event, such as a first-of-its-kind product launch with no historical precedent. What does this specific failure mode illustrate about a limitation of purely historical, pattern-based ML forecasting?

options.A: The failure proves the model must contain a fundamental coding defect unrelated to the nature of its training data
options.B: Backtesting performance on historical data always fully and reliably guarantees equally strong performance on any future, unprecedented scenario
options.C: A model trained purely on historical patterns has no inherent mechanism for anticipating genuinely unprecedented situations outside anything it has ever seen
options.D: Genuinely novel, unprecedented events can never meaningfully occur in any real-world retail forecasting context

questions.explanation: Because the model's learned patterns are entirely derived from historical precedent, it has nothing comparable to draw on for a genuinely unprecedented event, which is a structural limitation of purely historical, pattern-based forecasting rather than a coding bug, and argues for supplementing such models with human judgment for novel situations.

questions.question: A team testing a generative AI system for factual question-answering wants an evaluation approach more rigorous than simple human spot-checking, but a full independent ground-truth database for every possible question is infeasible to build. What testing strategy would give the strongest practical assurance under this constraint?

options.A: Abandoning any attempt at rigorous accuracy assessment and relying purely on user complaints after release to surface problems
options.B: Blanket review of trivial cases adds friction without improving real safety
options.C: Testing only the single easiest, most obviously answerable question, since it can serve as a full and complete oracle for every other question
options.D: Requiring the model to answer literally every possible question in existence before any release can occur

questions.explanation: When exhaustive ground truth is infeasible, a well-designed, risk-weighted sample, covering both common and high-stakes question types with real ground truth, gives meaningfully strong, generalizable assurance without needing infinite coverage.

questions.question: A tester designing acceptance tests for an AI-based system realizes that the business stakeholder's only stated requirement is "the AI should work well," with no further detail despite repeated requests for clarification. What is the most professionally appropriate next step for the tester?

options.A: Assume the requirement is now permanently and completely unattainable and recommend immediately canceling the entire project
options.B: The original scope may have missed a legally relevant characteristic
options.C: Proceed directly to writing detailed test cases based entirely on the tester's own personal, undiscussed guess about what "well" must mean
options.D: Refuse to test the system at all under any circumstances until a complete, perfect specification is provided in writing

questions.explanation: A vague acceptance criterion cannot be meaningfully tested against, so the professionally appropriate step is to actively work with the stakeholder to elicit concrete, measurable criteria, rather than guessing silently or refusing to engage with the ambiguity at all.

questions.question: A team's testing strategy for a generative AI system relies entirely on automated evaluation against a fixed benchmark dataset that has been publicly available online for over a year. What specific risk does public availability of the benchmark introduce for the credibility of reported results?

options.A: The age of a benchmark dataset has no bearing whatsoever on the credibility of results reported against it
options.B: Severity of the rare failure can reasonably outweigh the portability gain
options.C: Public benchmarks are always completely immune to ever being included in any model's training data
options.D: This risk applies only to benchmarks used for testing conventional, non-generative software systems

questions.explanation: A model trained on broad internet data could plausibly have encountered and partly memorized a long-public benchmark, which would inflate reported performance in a way that does not reflect genuine generalization, a known concern called benchmark contamination.

questions.question: A tester wants to verify that a chatbot's safety filter, which was primarily developed and tuned using English-language test cases, is equally effective when the same harmful requests are phrased in other languages the chatbot claims to support. What does neglecting this specific check risk missing?

options.A: This concern is only relevant for chatbots that support fewer than five total languages
options.B: Nothing meaningful, since a filter tuned in any single language is always guaranteed to generalize perfectly to every other supported language
options.C: Language-specific safety testing is a purely theoretical exercise with no real-world practical relevance whatsoever
options.D: A safety gap where the filter's protections do not transfer equally to non-English languages, leaving those users at greater risk from unfiltered harmful content

questions.explanation: Safety filtering behavior, especially if built on patterns learned mostly from English examples, may not transfer evenly to other languages, so testing only in English risks leaving a real, unaddressed safety gap for users of the chatbot's other supported languages.

questions.question: A team testing an AI system's explanations for its own decisions finds that the explanations are consistently plausible-sounding and well-formatted, but when the underlying input is deliberately changed in a way that should meaningfully alter the true decision-relevant factors, the generated explanation barely changes at all. What does this specific finding suggest?

options.A: A typical-user baseline can miss real gaps for the actual target group
options.B: This behavior is entirely expected and desirable for well-designed explanations, which should always remain constant regardless of any input change
options.C: The finding proves conclusively that the underlying decision model itself must contain a fundamental defect
options.D: Well-formatted, plausible-sounding explanations are always sufficient evidence of genuine explainability on their own

questions.explanation: A genuinely faithful explanation should shift when the actual decision-relevant factors shift; an explanation that stays static despite a meaningful change to those factors suggests it is a plausible-sounding narrative rather than one grounded in the model's real reasoning, a distinction this kind of targeted perturbation test specifically probes for.

questions.question: A tester is asked to sign off on the "adequacy" of testing for a new AI-based system but has not been given access to any information about how the training data was collected, cleaned or labeled, only the final trained model and its aggregate performance metrics. What is the strongest professional objection to signing off under these conditions?

options.A: Without visibility into the training data's provenance and quality, key risks such as bias, leakage or unrepresentativeness cannot be meaningfully assessed at all
options.B: No objection is warranted, since aggregate performance metrics alone are always fully sufficient evidence of comprehensive testing adequacy
options.C: The tester should sign off regardless, since requesting additional information would be considered unprofessional in this situation
options.D: Training data provenance is a purely academic concern with no genuine bearing on real testing adequacy in any practical context

questions.explanation: Many of the AI-specific risks this syllabus covers, from bias to leakage to representativeness, are only assessable with visibility into the training data itself; aggregate performance numbers alone cannot substitute for that visibility, making a sign-off under these conditions genuinely unsupportable.

questions.question: A team testing a generative AI system for legal document drafting establishes a rule: "if the system cites a law or case that does not actually exist, that is always a critical defect." A colleague argues this bar is "unrealistic" for any current generative AI system. How should a tester most appropriately respond to this specific objection?

options.A: Agree completely and lower the severity of fabricated legal citations to a minor cosmetic issue instead
options.B: Scaling helps fluency but not necessarily every quality dimension equally
options.C: Remove any testing for fabricated citations entirely, since the colleague's technical difficulty argument fully settles the matter
options.D: Conclude that generative AI can therefore never be used for any legal application under any circumstances whatsoever

questions.explanation: Technical difficulty in preventing an error does not change how severe its real-world consequences would be; a tester's job is to accurately classify risk and severity, which can validly stay high even for a hard-to-eliminate defect class, informing the release decision rather than being redefined away.

questions.question: A team's independent testing group is asked to test an AI system but is given only two days, compared with the many months the development team spent building and internally testing it. What is the most professionally sound way for the independent team to handle this significant resource mismatch?

options.A: Silently perform whatever testing is possible within the time given and report results with the same confidence as a fully resourced effort
options.B: Refuse to perform any testing at all, since anything less than an equally long effort as the development team's would be worthless
options.C: An implausible feature is a red flag for leaked label information
options.D: Artificially inflate the reported scope of testing performed to make the two-day effort appear equivalent to a much longer one

questions.explanation: Given a genuine resource mismatch, the professionally sound response is transparency: doing what is possible within the constraint while being explicit about what was and was not covered, so stakeholders can correctly calibrate their confidence rather than being misled about the depth of assurance actually provided.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A team collecting data to train a resume-screening model for technical roles discovers that their historical hiring data reflects a period when the company's technical workforce was overwhelmingly composed of graduates from a small handful of elite universities, due to past recruiting practices that have since changed. What is the most direct input-data testing concern this raises?

options.A: The concern only matters if literally every single hire during that historical period came from the same handful of universities
options.B: The training data may encode a narrow, historically contingent pattern that would unfairly disadvantage qualified candidates from different educational backgrounds
options.C: No concern exists, since historical hiring data is always, by definition, a fully representative and unbiased sample of qualified candidates
options.D: This is purely a historical curiosity with no bearing on how a model trained on this data would actually behave

questions.explanation: A model trained on data shaped by past, narrower recruiting practices risks learning that pattern as if it reflected genuine qualification, which is exactly the kind of historically contingent, potentially unfair signal input data testing should specifically investigate before training proceeds.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A team ingests a large public dataset for training a general-purpose image classifier and later discovers, through a licensing audit, that a portion of the images were scraped without proper rights or consent from the original creators. Beyond the direct legal exposure, what data-quality and testing concern does this discovery also raise?

options.A: No additional concern exists beyond the legal issue, since licensing problems never correlate with any other data-quality issue
options.B: Licensing audits and data-quality testing are always completely unrelated activities with no meaningful overlap
options.C: The concern only matters if the improperly sourced images make up more than 90% of the entire dataset
options.D: Fine-tuning here likely outperforms general scale on this narrow task

questions.explanation: A provenance problem discovered through a licensing audit often signals that a portion of the data was assembled without the same rigor as the rest, which reasonably raises questions about whether that same portion might also carry unaddressed quality or representativeness issues worth specifically investigating.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A tester validating a newly merged dataset, combining records from two previously separate systems after a company acquisition, finds that a "customer status" field uses different category codes with overlapping but non-identical meanings across the two source systems, with no documented mapping between them. What risk does training a model on this merged field, as-is, create?

options.A: The model may learn a distorted or meaningless pattern from a field that silently mixes several inconsistent, incompatible category schemes together
options.B: No risk exists, since merging any two datasets from different source systems always automatically resolves any category coding differences
options.C: This risk only matters if the merger involved more than three completely separate original source systems
options.D: Category code differences between merged systems never have any effect on how a supervised learning model performs

questions.explanation: Without a proper mapping, a field that silently blends genuinely different coding schemes effectively becomes an inconsistent, noisy signal, and a model trained on it directly risks learning spurious or contradictory patterns rather than the real underlying customer status.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A team preparing satellite imagery to train a crop-disease detection model finds that images from one particular region were consistently captured at a different time of day than images from other regions, due to satellite orbital scheduling, resulting in systematically different lighting and shadow patterns for that region's images. What subtle risk does this create?

options.A: Time-of-day capture differences are purely a cosmetic visual issue with no possible connection to a model's learned predictions
options.B: No risk exists, since lighting and shadow differences in satellite imagery never have any effect on how an image-based model learns
options.C: It has no way to tell a new legitimate pattern from a real threat
options.D: This risk can only ever occur if literally all of the images in the entire dataset were captured at the exact same time of day

questions.explanation: If a region-specific imaging artifact, like consistent lighting differences, happens to correlate with the actual outcome being predicted, the model risks latching onto that artifact as a shortcut instead of learning the genuine biological signal, a classic confounding risk in imagery-based ML.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A tester reviewing training data for a voice-based authentication system notices that all of the enrolled "reference" voice samples were recorded in a quiet studio environment, while real-world authentication attempts happen in varied, often noisy, everyday environments like streets or cafes. What input-data testing concern does this mismatch between enrollment and real-world conditions raise?

options.A: The system may perform poorly at real-world authentication if its notion of a "matching" voice was learned only from unrealistically clean reference conditions
options.B: No concern exists, since voice authentication systems are assumed to always perform identically regardless of any background environmental noise
options.C: This mismatch only matters if literally every single real-world authentication attempt happens to occur in an extremely loud environment
options.D: Studio-quality reference recordings always guarantee better real-world authentication accuracy than any noisier alternative would

questions.explanation: A large gap between the clean conditions used to build the reference voice profiles and the noisy conditions of real usage risks the system's matching behavior not transferring well, which is exactly the kind of representativeness gap between training and deployment conditions that input data testing should specifically flag.
